power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: COVID-19 provides an unprecedented opportunity to evaluate the contribution of public health and social measures (PHSMs) to controlling transmission and inform responses to future emerging respiratory pathogens.

We analysed SARS-CoV-2 transmission across 126 countries spanning multiple epidemic waves and diverse policy environments during periods when PHSMs were the primary interventions available to influence the epidemic.

By explicitly representing key epidemiological drivers of transmission and measuring reductions in residual transmission scaling after incorporating OxCGRT policy time-series data, we isolated the effect of PHSMs on transmission.
PHSMs frequently explained a substantial proportion of the observed variation in transmission intensity, with particularly strong effects seen in many high-income countries.
In countries with strong evidence for policy effects, reductions in transmission reached 60-80% or above, although the individual policies responsible for these effects varied considerably.
Harmonised analyses considering the effect of community mobility showed comparably strong effects in a similar subset of countries.

Preparedness against emerging respiratory pathogens remains a critical global challenge, as increasing environmental disruption and global connectedness create opportunities for pathogen emergence and spread. 1, 2 The COVID-19 pandemic provides the most important recent test of public health responses to such threats and so presents an unprecedented opportunity to evaluate the interventions used to control transmission. 3 While the effect of medical countermeasures such as vaccination can be more easily quantified through direct clinical investigations, understanding the effect of public health and social measures (PHSMs) must be largely inferred from epidemiological analyses. [4] [5] [6] As such, the scale, duration and geographic breadth of the PHSMs implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic provide an unparalleled opportunity to evaluate their contribution to controlling transmission and inform future responses to emerging respiratory pathogens.

text.text: Previous studies have generally concluded that PHSMs contributed to reductions in SARS-CoV-2 transmission, but have differed regarding the estimated magnitude of these effects and the relative importance of specific interventions. 5, [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] [12] These studies have variously identified stay-at-home orders, gathering restrictions, school closures and business restrictions as among the most effective measures, despite the inconsistency in the associated effect estimates.

text.text: These discrepancies may reflect differences in study settings, analysis periods, intervention packages and methodological approaches, including sensitivity to model specification. 13 Estimating policy effects from epidemic time series remains challenging because interventions are typically implemented in combination, vary across settings and become increasingly difficult to distinguish once medical countermeasures such as vaccination are introduced. 14, 15 Moreover, most previous analyses have been restricted to specific regions, subsets of countries or particular pandemic phases.
text.formatted: These discrepancies may reflect differences in study settings, analysis periods, intervention packages and methodological approaches, including sensitivity to model specification. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> Estimating policy effects from epidemic time series remains challenging because interventions are typically implemented in combination, vary across settings and become increasingly difficult to distinguish once medical countermeasures such as vaccination are introduced. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> Moreover, most previous analyses have been restricted to specific regions, subsets of countries or particular pandemic phases.

text.text: As a result, analyses that systematically integrate data across diverse geographic settings and throughout the period during which PHSMs constituted the primary response to the pandemic should provide a stronger basis for understanding the contribution of policy measures to transmission dynamics.
To address this challenge, we analysed SARS-CoV-2 transmission across 126 countries, encompassing multiple epidemic waves and diverse policy environments.

We developed a mechanistic framework to quantify the explanatory value of policy measures through reductions in residual transmission scaling when time series from the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker were incorporated into the analysis. 16 Applying this approach across all countries for which robust inference was possible, we present a globally comprehensive assessment of the extent to which PHSMs influenced transmission dynamics over the course of the pandemic.
text.formatted: We developed a mechanistic framework to quantify the explanatory value of policy measures through reductions in residual transmission scaling when time series from the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker were incorporated into the analysis. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> Applying this approach across all countries for which robust inference was possible, we present a globally comprehensive assessment of the extent to which PHSMs influenced transmission dynamics over the course of the pandemic.

text.text: We calibrated a renewal model with and without accounting for time series of policy changes to the COVID-19 epidemics of 126 countries.

By examining the extent to which including policy effects in the analysis reduced the need for residual nonmechanistic scaling of transmission, we quantified the evidence that policy changes influenced transmission in these settings.

The model incorporated epidemiological features including susceptible depletion, 17 variant-specific transmissibility, 18 incomplete immunity to emerging variants 19 and partial case ascertainment, 20 and we calibrated it to COVID-19 epidemiological targets that included time series profiles for weekly new deaths, case notifications, up to one hierarchically selected hospitalisation indicator and the proportional prevalence of key variants of concern.
text.formatted: The model incorporated epidemiological features including susceptible depletion, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> variant-specific transmissibility, <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> incomplete immunity to emerging variants <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> and partial case ascertainment, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> and we calibrated it to COVID-19 epidemiological targets that included time series profiles for weekly new deaths, case notifications, up to one hierarchically selected hospitalisation indicator and the proportional prevalence of key variants of concern.

text.text: For the baseline model, our methods matched those of our previous publication considering the effects of population mobility on transmission and focused on epidemiological contexts with low pre-existing natural immunity, including a later post-vaccination analysis window for Oceania and Singapore. 21 In the current analysis, we incorporated scaling for the effects of policy measures obtained from the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker (OxCGRT) database, which provides time series of severity for each of several policy indicators on ordinal scales. 16, 22 We achieved close matches to all calibration targets for each country under six approaches to scaling transmission: a baseline configuration with no scaling of transmission for policy effects, two alternative approaches to scaling for policy measures and three approaches to scaling for mobility inputs (Supplemental Files 2 and 3).

text.text: To motivate more formal analyses, we considered whether the OxCGRT time series appeared to track with the residual non-mechanistic scaling of transmission (henceforward "residual scaling") under the baseline model configuration that did not incorporate policy effects.

OxCGRT provides recommended sets of policies that can be combined to create overall indices of government policies, including the Containment and Stringency indices, and we constructed our own custom index for further analyses.

Supplemental File 4 and Figure 2 show comparisons of each of these three indices against baseline residual scaling using unweighted averages across policy domains (i.e. 1 ∑ , , where , represents the value of policy at time divided by its maximum value).
text.formatted: Supplemental File 4 and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> show comparisons of each of these three indices against baseline residual scaling using unweighted averages across policy domains (i.e. 1 ∑ , , where , represents the value of policy at time divided by its maximum value).

text.text: Although some countries showed little correspondence between variation in transmission and these composite policy time series (third column Figure 2), in many countries variation in transmission corresponded closely with the temporal trends of these indices (first two columns).
text.formatted: Although some countries showed little correspondence between variation in transmission and these composite policy time series (third column Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>), in many countries variation in transmission corresponded closely with the temporal trends of these indices (first two columns).

text.text: Our primary model configuration with policy effects included ("OxCGRT floored") incorporated weights for the contribution of each constituent policy to scaling, as well as a floor parameter for the maximum effect of policy changes and an exponential scaling parameter to map from the policy time series to the effect on transmission.
Supplemental File 6 and Figure 3 show the comparison between the residual transmission scaling (the same output as shown in Figure 2) and the calibrated policy scaling function after fitting to data.
text.formatted: Supplemental File 6 and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> show the comparison between the residual transmission scaling (the same output as shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>) and the calibrated policy scaling function after fitting to data.

text.text: This approach generated functions that closely matched residual transmission scaling in several settings (e.g.
Belgium, Aruba), suggesting that much of the unexplained variation in transmission captured by the residual process could alternatively be reproduced using policy information alone.
Supplemental File 6 and Figure 4 show the remaining residual scaling required after policy effects were included in the model.
text.formatted: Supplemental File 6 and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref> show the remaining residual scaling required after policy effects were included in the model.

text.text: If policy measures explain transmission dynamics, inclusion of policy scaling should reduce the residual need to adjust transmission.
Consistent with this expectation, the residual process became substantially flatter in most countries, with fewer abrupt fluctuations than under the baseline configuration.

We estimated the effect of policy changes on transmission by quantifying the reduction in variation in the residual process under the model configuration with scaling for policy effects compared to the baseline configuration without policy scaling.
To quantify this formally, we considered the dispersion parameter that governs the prior distributions for each update to the residual process compared to the preceding value.

This parameter was regularised by assigning a prior distribution with mode at zero to encourage the model to accept the minimum extent of residual scaling achievable while still matching the calibration targets.
Supplemental File 5 and the right-hand panels of Figure 5 show example posterior distributions for countries for which this dispersion parameter reduced substantially (e.g.
text.formatted: Supplemental File 5 and the right-hand panels of Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> show example posterior distributions for countries for which this dispersion parameter reduced substantially (e.g.

text.text: Norway), showed intermediate reduction (e.g.
Estonia) and for which there was little or no reduction (e.g.
Angola).

Because this parameter quantifies the magnitude of the residual adjustments required to fit observed epidemiological data, reductions in its posterior value indicate that policy data explain variation in transmission that would otherwise need to be captured by the residual process.
We therefore interpreted the proportion of calibration iterations under which this quantity reduced as the strength of evidence for an association between policies and transmission.

The left-hand panel of Figure 5 presents the results for all countries, showing strong evidence for an effect of policy changes in many high-income countries of Europe and North America, intermediate evidence in several countries of Eastern Europe, South America and Southern Africa, and minimal or no evidence for an effect in many countries of the rest of Africa and Oceania.
text.formatted: The left-hand panel of Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> presents the results for all countries, showing strong evidence for an effect of policy changes in many high-income countries of Europe and North America, intermediate evidence in several countries of Eastern Europe, South America and Southern Africa, and minimal or no evidence for an effect in many countries of the rest of Africa and Oceania.

text.text: Among the 52 high-income countries analysed, 29 showed a marked reduction in residual scaling (dispersion ratio reduced in 75% of runs or more), which was not seen in any of the 15 lowincome countries.

The strongest evidence was observed predominantly in European countries, including Poland, Greece, Slovenia, Luxembourg, Ireland, Czechia, Croatia, Romania, Austria, Sweden, Norway, Andorra, United Kingdom, Italy, Finland, France, Portugal, Switzerland, Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, Belgium, as well as Aruba, Israel, Cyprus, Japan, Canada, Bahamas, United States.
However, substantial evidence was also identified in several geographically heterogeneous middle-income countries, (e.g.

Eswatini, Belarus, Zimbabwe, Dominican Republic, Lesotho, Kosovo, South Africa, Iran, Nepal, Cuba, Moldova, Mexico, Tunisia, Serbia, Sri Lanka), possibly reflecting greater capacity to characterise transmission dynamics through routine surveillance in some of these countries.

We found no evidence for an effect of policy changes in countries for which our analysis spanned the post-vaccination roll-out Omicron period (Australia, New Zealand and Singapore), rather than the earlier pre-vaccination period considered in most of our analyses.

In countries for which there was little evidence for an effect of policy-related scaling of transmission, our alternative policy configuration (OxCGRT independent) performed less well than OxCGRT floored, because its priors were less able to support the absence of an effect.
We next quantified the maximum transmission reduction implied by the calibrated policy scaling function, 1 .

Although simultaneous implementation of all policies with the custom suite did not often occur during our analysis windows, we used this theoretical maximum scaling of transmission as our primary metric of the effectiveness of the overall policy package implemented in each country.
Figure 6 shows this estimate for the strength of policy effects across all countries analysed.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">6</ref> shows this estimate for the strength of policy effects across all countries analysed.

text.text: Because this metric is only meaningful when evidence for policy effects was detected, countries without such evidence are displayed in grey.
The strongest policy package effects were typically seen in high-income countries of Western and Northern Europe and North America, Japan and some countries of Southern Africa.
Intermediate effects were seen in some other African countries and several countries of South America and South Asia.
For several of the remaining African countries, as well as Oceania (for which the analysis period and methods differed), no evidence of an effect of policies on transmission was found.

To compare the effect of policy scaling to the effect of scaling for population mobility time series available from Google and Facebook, we adapted our previous mobility analyses for consistency with the policy analyses which are the primary objective of this manuscript.

We harmonised the scaling function for the mobility analyses with the function used for the policy analyses to include a "floor" parameter on the maximum reduction in the scaling process prior to the exponential transformation of the scaling function, whereas this floor was not incorporated in our previous mobilityfocused analyses.

Figure 7 shows that results for the policy and mobility analyses were strongly correlated, with strong effects of policy changes found in a similar group of countries as for those in which strong effects of mobility were observed.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">7</ref> shows that results for the policy and mobility analyses were strongly correlated, with strong effects of policy changes found in a similar group of countries as for those in which strong effects of mobility were observed.

text.text: Figure 8 compares the floor values between the policy and mobility analyses for the countries in which we found evidence of an effect under both of these analysis configurations.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">8</ref> compares the floor values between the policy and mobility analyses for the countries in which we found evidence of an effect under both of these analysis configurations.

text.text: For 39 of 50 countries under the Google comparison and for 36 of 52 under the Facebook comparison, the floor value for the mobility analysis was lower than for the policy analysis (by a median 8.5% and 7.2% respectively for the two analyses).
These findings suggest that mobility measures often captured a greater proportion of transmission-related behavioural change than policy measures alone.

Our main analysis (OxCGRT floored) approach assigned individual weights to each of the eight policies of our custom index, which were calibrated to create an overall weighted time series for the effect of policies on scaling transmission.
In many countries, specific policies were markedly upweighted by the calibration algorithm, such that the individual policy was assigned greater influence on the overall scaling function.
The posterior distributions of each policy weight for each country is shown in Supplemental File 10, with randomly selected country examples presented in Figure 9.
text.formatted: The posterior distributions of each policy weight for each country is shown in Supplemental File 10, with randomly selected country examples presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">9</ref>.

text.text: The relative extent of up-or down-weighting is presented in Figure 10, with restriction to countries for which there was evidence for an effect of the overall policy package and for which at least one policy was significantly up-or down-weighted.
text.formatted: The relative extent of up-or down-weighting is presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">10</ref>, with restriction to countries for which there was evidence for an effect of the overall policy package and for which at least one policy was significantly up-or down-weighted.

text.text: No policy displayed consistently strong effects across all countries, suggesting substantial heterogeneity in policy effectiveness and implementation contexts.
However, school closures often upweighted in countries of Europe and Asia, while movement restrictions were down-weighted in countries across several continents.

Across 126 countries spanning diverse policy environments and epidemic trajectories, policy stringency metrics provided substantial information regarding temporal variation in SARS-CoV-2 transmission intensity during periods when PHSMs were the primary pandemic response.

Incorporating policy data frequently reduced the model's need for residual transmission scaling, indicating that policy measures explained a substantial proportion of the variation in transmission beyond what was captured by the established epidemiological drivers we explicitly modelled.

Evidence for policy effects was strongest in many high-income countries of Europe and North America, although the magnitude of these effects and the policies most clearly associated with transmission varied considerably between settings.

Policy effects were easier to identify when interventions were analysed as an integrated package of measures rather than as independent effects, and the strength of their effects was often comparable to that observed for population mobility under equivalent analyses for the same countries.
Evidence for policy effects was strongly structured by economic setting and region.

Excluding the distinct epidemiological context of Oceania, policy signals were clearly identifiable across many high-income European and North American settings, but were largely absent in several low-income countries, particularly in Africa.

This inability to detect an effect mirrored our findings for mobility metrics, suggesting that failure to translate policy recommendations into population behavioural changes was unlikely to be the primary explanation.

Because the surveillance data typically provided clear epidemic trajectories despite lower case ascertainment estimates, non-detection is more likely to reflect misalignment between formal policy databases and on-the-ground implementation, rather than limitations in estimating transmission intensity itself.
Where policy effects were identifiable, they were often large.
In many high-income countries, particularly in Europe, the estimated maximum policy effect exceeded 0.6 and often reached 0.8 or above.

Under our modelling framework, this implies that the full package of non-pharmaceutical interventions represented in the OxCGRT database could reduce transmission by 60-80% or more when implemented simultaneously at maximum intensity.
These estimates reflect the maximum potential weighted effect of the intervention packages, rather than the independent effect of individual measures.
While stronger policy effects were moderately associated with higher gross domestic product and some geographic clustering was observed, these relationships were not homogeneous.

This suggests that local country-specific factors, such as differences in background contact structures, policy implementation, community uptake and capacity to adhere to recommendations, played an important role in determining policy effectiveness.
Countries with strong evidence for policy effects generally also showed strong mobility effects.

This was particularly evident when mobility was measured using the Facebook metric describing the number of 600 m × 600 m tiles visited, although similar patterns were observed using Google's location-based mobility indicators.

This concordance is intuitive, given that many of the non-pharmaceutical interventions included in our analysis are expected to influence transmission primarily through reductions in population movement and social contact patterns. 23 Despite this alignment, the estimated transmission floor parameter () was on average 12% lower under mobility models than policy models.
text.formatted: This concordance is intuitive, given that many of the non-pharmaceutical interventions included in our analysis are expected to influence transmission primarily through reductions in population movement and social contact patterns. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> Despite this alignment, the estimated transmission floor parameter () was on average 12% lower under mobility models than policy models.

text.text: This could plausibly reflect the theoretical bound of mobility data -where near-zero movement would conceptually imply a near absence of transmission -whereas policy models achieve equivalent observed transmission reductions by steepening the scaling response (via the exponent mapping parameter ) while maintaining a higher baseline floor of contact.

A further notable finding was that specific interventions were often identified as important contributors to transmission control within a given country, although the specific policies selected varied markedly between settings.

This heterogeneity implies that the apparent effectiveness of individual interventions was strongly influenced by the local context and implementation approach, rather than supporting a single set of universally effective policies.

Policy indicators were highly correlated on principal component analysis of the raw policy time series values, with the first principal component explaining a median of 58% of temporal variation across countries.

This limited the extent to which independent policy effects could be disentangled and reflects the fact that interventions were typically implemented as part of broader policy responses rather than in isolation.
We therefore placed greater emphasis on results from the policy-package formulation (OxCGRT floored), which is more consistent with these implementation patterns.

Furthermore, the package formulation allowed the overall policy effect to approach zero, whereas the independent policy formulation effectively required all policy effects to approach zero simultaneously to infer no effect.

Consequently, our findings provide stronger evidence that changes in the overall policy response influenced transmission than for a single set of intervention-specific effects that generalises across settings.

Early studies of the effects of PHSMs inferred variation in transmission from the first epidemic wave of SARS-CoV-2 and were influential in guiding the initial response to COVID-19. 5, [7] [8] [9] [10] Our analysis advances from these works by analysing how PHSMs dynamically influenced multiple waves of transmission that were driven by heterogeneous variants of SARS-CoV-2 and span repeated cycles of policy implementation and relaxation.
text.formatted: Early studies of the effects of PHSMs inferred variation in transmission from the first epidemic wave of SARS-CoV-2 and were influential in guiding the initial response to COVID-19. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> Our analysis advances from these works by analysing how PHSMs dynamically influenced multiple waves of transmission that were driven by heterogeneous variants of SARS-CoV-2 and span repeated cycles of policy implementation and relaxation.

text.text: A study of European countries spanning the first two waves of COVID-19 found effects of PHSMs often declined over these phases of the epidemic, supporting our finding that these effects were not constant over time and depended on the local epidemiological and policy context. 11 These previous studies frequently estimated substantial effects of PHSMs but arrived at differing conclusions regarding the effectiveness of individual measures.
text.formatted: A study of European countries spanning the first two waves of COVID-19 found effects of PHSMs often declined over these phases of the epidemic, supporting our finding that these effects were not constant over time and depended on the local epidemiological and policy context. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> These previous studies frequently estimated substantial effects of PHSMs but arrived at differing conclusions regarding the effectiveness of individual measures.

text.text: Our findings suggest that this variation may reflect both differences in the ability of available data to capture policyrelated effects on transmission across settings and that policy packages are more readily identifiable than the effects of individual measures.

Consistent with several past studies we found that mobility and transmission often varied in concert, and further show that the countries with strongest effects of mobility and of policies often coincided. 21, 24, 25 Limitations of our study include that the OxCGRT input data pertain to policy recommendations rather than compliance, 26 which we mitigated by comparing to equivalent analyses of the effects of mobility.
text.formatted: Consistent with several past studies we found that mobility and transmission often varied in concert, and further show that the countries with strongest effects of mobility and of policies often coincided. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> Limitations of our study include that the OxCGRT input data pertain to policy recommendations rather than compliance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> which we mitigated by comparing to equivalent analyses of the effects of mobility.

text.text: Our national-level framework did not capture subnational policy variation, which may be substantial in large or federated countries, 27, 28 though we sought to mitigate this by analysing periods of widespread community transmission rather than localised outbreak responses.
text.formatted: Our national-level framework did not capture subnational policy variation, which may be substantial in large or federated countries, <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> though we sought to mitigate this by analysing periods of widespread community transmission rather than localised outbreak responses.

text.text: Because many interventions were implemented concurrently, our primary analysis considered policies as packages, and we did not find consistent evidence for the independent effects of specific interventions across all countries.
Further, the policies we considered were largely restricted to face-covering requirements and measures expected to influence attendance at workplaces, schools and other community venues.

Other behaviours that may influence transmission, including voluntary behavioural responses to changing epidemic conditions, were not explicitly represented and so may contribute to residual unexplained variation. 29 Policy measures substantially influenced SARS-CoV-2 transmission across many countries during periods in which PHSMs formed the primary public health response.
text.formatted: Other behaviours that may influence transmission, including voluntary behavioural responses to changing epidemic conditions, were not explicitly represented and so may contribute to residual unexplained variation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> Policy measures substantially influenced SARS-CoV-2 transmission across many countries during periods in which PHSMs formed the primary public health response.

text.text: Using a framework based on the reduction in residual transmission scaling required to fit epidemiological data, we identified strong evidence that policy measures explained variation in transmission beyond that captured by established epidemiological drivers.

The close correspondence between policy-and mobilitybased analyses suggests that much of this effect was mediated through changes in population behaviour, although behavioural influences on transmission appear to extend beyond those directly attributable to formal policy measures.

While the magnitude of policy effects varied considerably between settings, our findings demonstrate that policy signals remained detectable across multiple epidemic waves, SARS-CoV-2 variants and epidemiological contexts.
Our full methods are presented in Supplemental File 1 and summarised as follows.
We used a renewal model with daily time innovations and a gamma-distributed generation interval to simulate the COVID-19 epidemic of 126 countries independently.

The model incorporated key epidemiological features, including susceptible depletion, multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants of varying transmissibility and severity, partial cross immunity following past infection with a different variant and incomplete case ascertainment.

The variant-specific force of infection is calculated as: , , ,, , Where represents the baseline transmissibility of SARS-CoV-2, while captures the relative infectiousness of each variant. is a Wiener process with weekly updates and is a policy scaling function, which is explained further below. , is the seeding function for variant and is the gamma-distributed generation interval distribution.
To incorporate policy effects, we constructed a time-varying transmission scaling function (Figure 1).
text.formatted: To incorporate policy effects, we constructed a time-varying transmission scaling function (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Under our primary analysis configuration ("OxCGRT floored"), each policy indicator contributed to a combined policy intensity measure, which was then transformed using floor and exponent parameters to produce the final transmission scaling factor.
Where , is the ratio of the policy time series from OxCGRT for the individual policy at time to its maximum ordinal value and is a policy-specific calibrated weight (such that , " #0, 1%).

Our custom policy index comprised the following eight indicators: school closing, workplace closing, cancel public events, gathering restrictions, close public transport, stay at home, movement restrictions and face coverings (OxCGRT codes C1 to C7 and H6).

This suite of policies is intended to represent policies that may influence local transmission, except that it excluded public information because this showed almost no variation during the analysis periods considered.
As such, our weighted policy indicator provides a per-country modified stringency index, where individual policies contribute to the index based on their empirical influence on case numbers.

This differs from the OxCGRT stringency index, which includes international travel and public information but not face coverings and calculates stringency as the simple average of all contributing components. and are the floor and exponent parameters respectively, which are used to map from the weighted average of policy stringencies to the overall effect on transmission.

We also considered an alternative configuration ("OxCGRT independent") which considered each policy as having an independent effect rather than acting as part of a policy package, and is calculated as ∑ & , , , where & is a calibrated parameter for the independent effect of policy on transmission and the raw OxCGRT value is normalised to its starting value.

text.text: Last, we also considered an equivalent analysis considering the effects of mobility instead of policies, but adopted a new approach to calculating from our previous work to align better with the policy scaling approach (incorporating floor and exponent parameters).

Gamma-distributed convolution functions were applied to the infection values calculated from the transmission model above to estimate weekly cases, hospitalisations and deaths, with the parameters to these distributions estimated during calibration from informative literature-based priors.
We calculated our likelihood by comparing each of these model outputs against the corresponding calibration targets using a normal distribution in log space.

We also fit to estimates of seroprevalence in our calibration algorithm where available to mildly constrain the total epidemic size, but assigned this target a lower weight in the calculation of our overall likelihood.

We implemented the model using Google's jax library and calibrated using numpyro's NUTS algorithm. 30, 31 Inference The primary purpose of our analysis was to estimate the extent to which the need for residual scaling declined with the inclusion of the policy scaling.

text.text: We assessed policy effects by quantifying changes in the dispersion parameter governing the Wiener process ' .

This parameter determines how freely the residual transmission scaling process can vary over time, with larger values permitting greater temporal fluctuations in residual scaling and smaller values implying less unexplained variation after accounting for mechanistically modelled drivers.
We assigned this parameter a half-normal prior distribution with standard deviation 0.5 to penalise greater jumps to each successive value, and so discourage unnecessary non-mechanistic variation.
As such, we considered the posterior distribution of the dispersion parameter to represent the strength of evidence for an effect of policies on transmission.
Further, when all policies were implemented at their maximum level the transmission scaling function reduces to .
As such, we took 1 to represent the maximum possible policy-related effect on transmission under the floored analysis approach.
We interpreted the floor parameter as the proportion of transmission-relevant behaviours that could not be eliminated through changes to policies or mobility.
For interpretation of the individual policy weights, we used the quantity ( log ,-. 1 / 0 -1 /2 as our primary metric of whether a policy was up-or down-weighted, and set / at 0.1.

Because each pre-normalisation policy-specific weight was assigned a uniform prior distribution on #0, 1%, the prior expectation of ( is equal to zero, with positive values indicating that the posterior distribution is skewed towards one and negative values indicating skew towards zero.
